messages.subject: Best Practices: Reactivity
parts:
How do you guys structure efficient code? I find that I write a lot of stuff that ends up working but I'm unconvinced it is the most efficient way of doing things.
For instance, I have a lot of code in server.r that looks like

output$title1 <- renderText({
if (is.null(input$x)| is.null(input$y)) {return(invisible())}
temp <- myfunction(reactiveThing())       #reactiveThing depends of input$x and input$y
sprintf('myNumber is %s', temp)
})

I find that in order to eliminate errors I have to throw {return(invisible())} all over the place. Is that a good idea or am I missing a better way of managing dependencies?
Also, and I'm not sure if this is related, I find that if a tab has a couple reactive elements, that they respond to changes at different times and will often display my error messages like

output$Error <- renderText({
if (is.null(input$x) | is.null(input$y)) {return(invisible())}
if(nrow(reactiveTable()) < 1) {return('No Data within Date Range for this View')} #reactiveTable is dependent on x and y
})

for a moment and then get reset.

I know this is a collection of specific and vague questions but I was hoping to get a better sense of good practices.
Kind of like a style guide to reactivity in shiny.

thanks!

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Best Practices: Reactivity
parts: Hi Andres, thanks for the thoughtful and detailed questions.
> I find that in order to eliminate errors I have to throw {return(invisible())} all over the place.

Rather than testing on input$x and input$y for null, I tend to have each chunk of code only test for null on its direct dependencies--in this case, reactiveThing. (Note that it's relatively cheap to call reactiveThing() twice since it automatically caches its results.)

That being said, I don't think this situation is ideal, since the whole chain of dependencies needs to have this "Is it null? then return NULL" logic. I've been thinking for a while that we should have a special condition/error that indicates that a calculation is missing its prerequisites, so that reactiveThing() could be something like

reactiveThing <- reactive({
  if (is.null(input$x) || is.null(input$y)) {
    signalCancel()
  }
  # Do stuff...
})

where signalCancel would essentially throw a unique error that doesn't show up in the UI as a red error message. That way, anything that directly or indirectly depends on reactiveThing would automatically inherit this behavior, unless they explicitly wrap that part of the code with tryCatch or whatever.

Would welcome any thoughts about this.

As for the second part of your e-mail, if you mean that when you switch between tabs you sometimes see old/stale results before they update, that is probably because by default outputs are lazy-loading; if they are not visible, they don't recalculate. You can change this behavior on an output-by-output basis by using outputOptions, specifically the suspendWhenHidden option.

messages.subject: Re: Best Practices: Reactivity
parts:
Joe:

I assume you mean that you put the is.null(input$x) inside reactiveThing(). myfunction then has to check if the return from reactiveThing is a null. 

Caching of reactives is great but if reactiveThing returns a big datasets calling it is not that cheap ... or is it?

Not having the red-errors pop-up would be great :)
